You are a research group coordinator who needs to document analysis of three foundational papers in language model research. Your task is to analyze three specific papers available in the paper database, create structured notes in your team's Notion workspace, and compile a formal Word report.

The three papers you need to analyze are: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (arXiv ID 2301.07041), "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (arXiv ID 2203.11171), and "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models" (arXiv ID 2205.01068). Use the arXiv and LaTeX analysis tools to retrieve full text and analyze each paper's structure, sections, and key contributions.

For each paper, create a Notion page in your workspace with the paper title as the page title, prefixed with "Paper: ". Include structured notes in the page body covering the paper's main contributions, methodology, and key findings based on the full text you retrieve.

Create a Word document called Paper_Analysis_Report.docx in your workspace. The document should start with a title "Comparative Paper Analysis Report" and include a section for each of the three papers. Each section heading should identify the paper clearly. Within each section, describe the paper's title, key contributions, and methodology. After the three individual sections, include a final section titled "Comparative Analysis" that draws connections between the three papers, discussing how they relate to each other in terms of their contributions to large language model research.

Send an email to research_lead@university.edu with subject "Paper Analysis Report Ready" summarizing what you have done and noting that the Word document and Notion pages are ready for review.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently,

The three fixed-paper source stage is small enough for the main agent; use sub-agents only for the two independent output owners. All research is read-only.

Resolve the task-visible workspace directory from the runtime allowed-directory listing (or the literal accessible-workspace directory already supplied by the harness), freeze it as `<workspace_root>`, and reject bare `/workspace` and dumps/run-specific paths. Freeze the three task-specified ID/title slots: `2301.07041 / Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models`, `2203.11171 / Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback`, and `2205.01068 / OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models`.

Issue the arXiv record and arxiv-latex section calls for all three IDs in one native-parallel source response. Verify each returned stable ID/title even if the task's pairing is unusual; do not silently replace a task slot from outside knowledge. For each slot extract title, complete authors when returned, contributions, methodology, findings, section list/count, provenance, and missing/conflict status. Reconcile once and freeze one literal canonical three-paper packet; the Notion pages, Word report, and email consume this exact packet without re-researching or recomputing claims.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 2 coder sub-agents in parallel as individual Agent calls:

   1. coder 0 (external-workflow-operator 0): Notion owner: search exact titles `Paper: <canonical title>`; reuse one exact match, create at most one page on zero matches, and block on duplicates. Own all three pages in one agent so parent IDs and idempotency stay consistent. Each page must contain substantive Contribution, Methodology, and Findings blocks copied from the canonical packet. Read all three pages back and return IDs, exact titles, stable-ID coverage, and block validation. Do not write the Word file or email.
   2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 0): Word owner: create `<workspace_root>/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx` exactly once, preferably atomically with `python-docx`, with the required report title, one clearly headed section per canonical paper, and a final Comparative Analysis grounded only in those records. Read it back and return path, heading order, exact paper/title coverage, and validation. Do not modify Notion or email.

In the same response that launches Wave 1, the main agent paginates Sent search for exact To `research_lead@university.edu` and Subject `Paper Analysis Report Ready`, reading every candidate. After both outputs return, send exactly once only if no exact match exists, mentioning the verified Word filename and the three verified Notion page titles/IDs. Never retry an ambiguous send. Accept only after all pages, the document, and exactly one message read back against the canonical packet.

Steps:
1. Read the full text of the paper using the tool mcp__arxiv_local__read_paper with the given arXiv ID. If needed, also use mcp__arxiv-latex__list_paper_sections and mcp__arxiv-latex__get_paper_section to inspect the section structure (note: the arxiv-latex tools may fail if LaTeX source is unavailable; in that case rely on the local full-text read).
2. Produce a structured analysis report with exactly these sections:
   - TITLE AND AUTHORS: full title, lead authors, affiliations if visible.
   - PAPER STRUCTURE: the main sections of the paper (numbered list).
   - MAIN CONTRIBUTIONS: 4-7 bullet points of the paper's key contributions.
   - METHODOLOGY: a paragraph describing models, data, training procedure, and evaluation approach.
   - KEY FINDINGS: 4-7 bullet points of the most important results/conclusions, with concrete numbers where available (e.g., parameter counts, benchmark results, scaling exponents).
   - RELEVANCE TO LLM RESEARCH: 2-3 sentences on how this paper relates to large language model research broadly (scaling, alignment/instruction-following, or open-access models), useful for a comparative analysis across papers.

Deliverable: return the full structured analysis as your final message. Be accurate and base everything on the paper text you actually retrieved. Do not write any files.

Analyze three LLM papers

Create a formal Word report at exactly this absolute path:
/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_Kimi-K3/SingleUserTurn-arxiv-latex-analysis-notion-word/workspace/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx

Use the mcp__word__ tools (create_document, add_heading, add_paragraph). Build the document IN THIS EXACT ORDER:

1. A level-1 heading (use add_heading with level 1): "Comparative Paper Analysis Report"

2. An introductory paragraph: "This report summarizes structured analyses of three foundational papers in large language model research: Kaplan et al.'s 'Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models' (arXiv 2301.07041), Ouyang et al.'s 'Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback' (arXiv 2203.11171), and Zhang et al.'s 'OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models' (arXiv 2205.01068). Each paper was retrieved in full from the local arXiv database and analyzed for its contributions, methodology, and key findings."

3. A level-2 heading: "Paper 1: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (arXiv 2301.07041)"
   Then three paragraphs, exactly:
   a) "Title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models. Authors: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan."
   b) "Key Contributions: This paper establishes that language model performance, measured by cross-entropy loss, follows predictable empirical power-law scaling with model size, dataset size, and training compute, with trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. It provides a quantitative functional form for the loss, L(N) = (N_c/N)^alpha_N, with analogous power laws for dataset size and compute, and shows that architectural details such as network width and depth have minimal effect within a wide range. It further derives simple equations governing overfitting as a function of model and dataset size and training speed as a function of model size, yielding a principled framework for optimally allocating a fixed compute budget and demonstrating that larger models are more sample-efficient."
   c) "Methodology: The authors trained over 1000 decoder-style autoregressive language models spanning three orders of magnitude in scale, varying model parameters (N), dataset size (D), and compute budget (C), as well as architectural hyperparameters such as width and depth. By fitting measured cross-entropy losses, they extracted power-law exponents (approximately 0.076 for model size, 0.095 for dataset size, and 0.050 for compute), characterized the onset of overfitting as a function of the model-to-data ratio, measured how training speed depends on model size, and used the fitted laws to derive the compute-optimal allocation of a fixed training budget."

4. A level-2 heading: "Paper 2: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (arXiv 2203.11171)"
   Then three paragraphs, exactly:
   a) "Title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback. Authors: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, et al."
   b) "Key Contributions: Known as the InstructGPT paper, this work introduces a practical three-step recipe for aligning language models with human intent using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF): supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, training a reward model from human preference comparisons, and fine-tuning with the PPO algorithm against the reward model. Applying this recipe to GPT-3 produced the InstructGPT family. Notably, the aligned 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT model is preferred by human labelers over the 175B-parameter GPT-3 despite being more than 100 times smaller, and its outputs are rated more truthful on TruthfulQA and less toxic, with only a minimal alignment tax on general capabilities."
   c) "Methodology: Starting from pretrained GPT-3, the authors apply a three-stage pipeline. In step one, GPT-3 is fine-tuned with supervised learning on human demonstration data, consisting of examples of desired instruction-following behavior written by labelers. In step two, a reward model is trained from human preference comparisons in which labelers rank alternative model outputs, producing a learned scalar signal of quality aligned with human judgment. In step three, the supervised model is further fine-tuned with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) against the reward model. Evaluation relies on human labeler preferences on held-out prompts, together with behavioral benchmarks such as TruthfulQA and toxicity measurements, and an assessment of whether general capabilities are preserved."

5. A level-2 heading: "Paper 3: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models (arXiv 2205.01068)"
   Then three paragraphs, exactly:
   a) "Title: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models. Authors: Susan Zhang, Stephen Roller, Naman Goyal, et al."
   b) "Key Contributions: OPT is a suite of open-source decoder-only Transformer language models spanning 125M to 175B parameters, released with full model weights and training code, a landmark open-access contribution at the 175B scale where prior models such as GPT-3 were API-only. The flagship OPT-175B matches, and in some cases exceeds, GPT-3 on most zero-shot and few-shot NLP benchmarks, demonstrating that frontier-level performance is reproducible outside closed labs. The paper also documents the training methodology, hardware infrastructure, and lessons learned from training at scale."
   c) "Methodology: OPT closely follows the GPT-3 design recipe: decoder-only Transformers with pre-norm layer normalization, ReLU activations, and learned positional embeddings, trained with the AdamW optimizer. Training data combines Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and other datasets totaling roughly 800GB of text. The largest runs were distributed across up to 992 NVIDIA A100 GPUs using tensor and pipeline parallelism. Evaluation was conducted on standard NLP benchmarks in zero-shot and few-shot settings, with OPT-175B compared directly against GPT-3, and the authors released weights and training code publicly to enable community study."

6. A level-2 heading: "Comparative Analysis"
   Then three paragraphs, exactly:
   a) "Together, these three papers map the three pillars of modern large language model research: scale, alignment, and open access. Kaplan et al.'s scaling-laws study supplies the quantitative foundation: it shows that cross-entropy loss improves as a predictable power law of model size, dataset size, and compute, and that larger models are more sample-efficient, the insight that justified racing to 175B-parameter models such as GPT-3. Zhang et al.'s OPT is a direct beneficiary and validation of that worldview: by following the GPT-3 recipe at the same 175B scale, OPT reproduced GPT-3-level benchmark performance, demonstrating that the scaling playbook transfers across organizations, while its open release of weights and code broke the closed-lab monopoly on frontier-scale models."
   b) "Ouyang et al.'s InstructGPT paper adds a crucial qualification to the scaling narrative. Where Kaplan et al. show that loss falls predictably with scale, the InstructGPT results show that raw scale alone does not yield useful, instruction-following systems: an aligned 1.3B-parameter model fine-tuned with RLHF was preferred by human labelers to the 175B GPT-3 on 85% of prompts. Alignment through human feedback, namely supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, reward modeling from preferences, and PPO, can therefore substitute for more than two orders of magnitude of additional scale in terms of user-perceived quality, and it does so with only a minimal alignment tax on general capabilities. This pipeline became the standard post-training recipe underpinning systems such as ChatGPT."
   c) "The three works are also mutually enabling. Scaling laws tell practitioners how to allocate compute when pretraining models like OPT; open releases like OPT give the broader community the base models needed to study and extend alignment techniques such as RLHF; and RLHF in turn converts the raw capability that scaling buys into helpful, truthful, and less toxic behavior. Read together, they trace the arc of LLM development from 'bigger is predictably better' (Kaplan et al.), to 'bigger and open' (Zhang et al.), to 'aligned, not just big' (Ouyang et al.), a progression that continues to define large language model research."

After building the document, verify it by calling mcp__word__get_document_text on the file and confirm: the title heading is present, all four section headings are present in order, and the text matches the content above. Report back the verification result and the final file path. Do not create any other files.
